name: Rome as culturally 'parasitic' on Greece
plain_explanation: Russell argues Rome, despite conquering the Mediterranean world militarily, invented essentially no new art form, philosophy, or scientific discovery of its own; educated Romans instead learned Greek, imitated Greek architecture and sculpture, borrowed Greek philosophical schools wholesale, and even invented a legendary Trojan ancestry to link themselves to Greek myth.
precise_definition: Russell's characterization of the direction of Greco-Roman cultural dependency: Rome contributed genuine originality in roads, legal codes, and military/administrative organization, but relied on Greece for art, literature, philosophy, and science throughout its history.
why_it_mattered: Explains why the intellectual history of the Roman period (outside law and engineering) is largely the continuing, if declining, history of Greek thought under Roman political conditions rather than a new, independently Roman philosophical tradition.
historical_origin: Traced from the Roman elite's post-Punic-War infatuation with Greek culture (language, architecture, sculpture, mythology, philosophy).
examples: Roman gods identified with Greek gods
The invented Trojan origin myth of Rome, linking it to Homeric legend
competing_positions: Rome's genuine areas of originality: 'good roads, systematic legal codes, and efficient armies'
